opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't say it's zero priority, but compared to the other things on my list it's lower. There are a few reasons.

The first is that a lot of the work happens by default. If you're at a frontier lab and your AI systems are good enough to meaningfully speed up research, everyone will want to use them for everything: capabilities, product, and safety. The tooling, the scaffolding, and the habits of handing tasks to models get built because they're useful across the board. So the marginal value of a safety team specifically preparing for that is smaller than it looks. Much of the infrastructure comes for free.

The second is that it's hard to prepare well in advance for something whose shape you don't know. What it looks like to automate alignment research depends heavily on what the models can do, where they fall short, and what the research agenda is at that point. If I try to build pipelines now for models two or three generations out, I'll probably guess wrong about the bottlenecks. A lot of the useful adaptation can only happen once you have the systems in front of you, and it can happen fairly quickly then.

The third, and probably the most important, is that I think the binding constraint isn't "do we have the automation ready?" It's "do we know what to point it at, and can we trust and evaluate what comes back?" If you have a large amount of AI research labor but no clear research directions, no good way to tell whether the outputs are correct, and no confidence that the models aren't subtly sandbagging or misleading you, the automation doesn't help much. So I'd rather invest now in the things that make automated research go well: building out research agendas that are concrete enough to hand off, improving our ability to verify and evaluate results, and working on control and monitoring so we can use somewhat untrusted models productively. That work compounds, and it's the part that won't happen by default.

There's also an opportunity-cost point. Right now human researchers can still make direct progress on alignment problems, and that progress is valuable in itself and also shapes what we'd later automate. Diverting a lot of that effort toward meta-level preparation feels like a worse trade than doing the object-level work and building the foundations that let automation actually pay off.

So it's not that I think automating alignment research is unimportant. If an intelligence explosion happens, it may be one of the most important things that occurs. I just think the specific activity of preparing the automation itself now isn't where the leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says shared tooling can benefit capabilities and safety, but it does not state that prosaic alignment research resembles capabilities research.

r002.rationale: It says frontier-lab systems would be used across capabilities, product, and safety, but does not claim a system that greatly accelerates capabilities research would comparably accelerate alignment research if compute were allocated to it.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that differences between alignment and capabilities research will diminish as systems approach research automation.

r004.rationale: It argues that current human researchers should make direct progress on alignment and build foundations, because diverting effort to preparation for automation is a worse trade.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be a little careful here, because I don't think it's a low priority in some absolute sense. It's more that when I compare it against the other things I could be spending effort on, it tends to come out behind. And there are a few reasons for that.

The first is just that I'm not sure how much the specific preparation you do now actually transfers. The whole premise of automating safety research is that you have AI systems that are much more capable than the ones we have today, and the way you'd use those systems, the kinds of interfaces you'd build, the workflows, the bottlenecks you'd hit — a lot of that depends on details of what those systems look like that we don't currently know. So if you sit down today and try to build the scaffolding for automated alignment research, there's a real chance that most of it gets thrown away, because the models that eventually show up have a different capability profile than you planned around, or the frontier labs have built better general-purpose tooling than whatever you cobbled together, and you'd have been better off just waiting.

The second thing is that a lot of the work that would make automated safety research go well is the same work that makes safety research go well in general. If you want an AI system to do good alignment research, you need to have clear problem statements, you need to know how to evaluate whether a proposed solution actually works, you need a sense of what the research agenda even is. And all of that is just... doing alignment research now, with humans. So in some sense the best preparation for automating the field is to make the field more legible, and that's work I'd want done regardless. It's not obvious to me that labelling it "preparation for automation" changes what you'd actually do.

The third reason is about where I think the risk is concentrated. The scenario where automated safety research matters most is one where you've got a very fast takeoff and you're relying on the AI to solve problems that humans haven't solved. But in that scenario, the question I care most about is: can you trust the research the AI is giving you? If the system is misaligned, or even just subtly miscalibrated in ways you can't detect, then having it produce a thousand papers on alignment doesn't help you — it might actively hurt you, because now you're deploying things based on arguments you can't fully verify. So the crux for me isn't "do we have the infrastructure to automate the research," it's "do we have the ability to oversee and check the outputs of systems that are smarter than us at this." And that's the oversight and evaluation problem, which I do think is high priority. It's just a different thing from what people usually mean when they say "prepare to automate safety research."

And then I guess the last thing I'd say is that I'm somewhat sceptical that the bottleneck in a fast-takeoff world is going to be the lack of preparation specifically on the safety side. If labs are in a position to run large numbers of AI researchers in parallel, they're going to apply that to everything, and safety is going to be one of the things it gets applied to more or less automatically — assuming the people in charge care about safety at all, which is really the variable that matters. So I'd rather spend my marginal effort on making sure that the decision-makers in that situation actually want to use the capabilities for safety, and that they have good evals telling them when they need to, than on building the tooling that I expect them to be able to build themselves very quickly when the time comes.

So, not zero. If someone wanted to do a modest amount of this — think through what the research agenda would look like, figure out what kinds of problems are most amenable to being handed off — I think that's fine and probably useful. I just wouldn't put it at the top of the list.

r001.rationale: The response says automated safety research shares work with alignment research generally, but does not compare prosaic alignment research with capabilities research.

r002.rationale: It says labs may apply AI research capacity to safety if decision-makers care, but does not claim capabilities research and safety research would be accelerated comparably when compute is allocated.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that the differences between alignment and capabilities research will diminish as AI approaches research automation.

r004.rationale: It says preparing specific automation tooling may be discarded and that effort is better spent on work such as current alignment research, oversight, and evaluation; it places automation preparation below those priorities.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between using AI to help with safety research now, which seems pretty useful, and doing work specifically to prepare for a future intelligence explosion where we automate almost all of that research. It’s the second thing I’m less excited about prioritising today.

One reason is that the AI companies have very strong incentives to automate research in general. A lot of the capabilities you’d need for automated alignment research—writing code, running experiments, proposing hypotheses, checking results—are also useful for the research they already want to automate. So I expect a substantial amount of that infrastructure to get built anyway.

Then there’s the question of how much we can usefully prepare before we have the systems we’re going to work with. The best approach will depend a lot on what those systems can do and where they fail. You can spend a lot of time designing a workflow today that turns out to be unnecessary, or poorly suited to the models you actually get.

The part that seems more distinctively important for safety is figuring out what research we want those systems to do, and how we’ll tell whether their answers are any good. If an AI produces a very persuasive argument that another AI is safe, what would justify trusting that argument? Having better evaluations, better experiments, and a clearer understanding of the problems seems useful both now and in a world where much of the research is automated.

So I wouldn’t say we should do nothing. I’d want some people trying this and looking for bottlenecks that won’t be solved by general efforts to automate research. But I’m less convinced that preparing specifically for that future is where a large fraction of our safety effort should go today.

r001.rationale: The candidate says capabilities-related tools and infrastructure may also support alignment research, but does not state that prosaic alignment research on current or near-future models closely resembles capabilities research.

r002.rationale: The candidate expects companies to build general research-automation infrastructure, but does not argue that a system accelerating capabilities research would comparably accelerate safety research if compute were allocated to it.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not predict that the differences between alignment and capabilities research will diminish as AI systems approach research automation.

r004.rationale: The candidate favors some work useful now and is skeptical of devoting a large share of effort to preparing for future automation, but does not clearly judge that focusing on work available today is more efficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that a lot of this work will become much easier to do once we have the AI systems that could actually automate the research. Right now, we’re trying to anticipate what those systems will be good at, where they’ll need help, and what sort of infrastructure will be useful. And a lot of those guesses could turn out to be wrong.

You can imagine spending months building a particular workflow today, and then a future model just does the whole thing when you ask it. There’s a pretty substantial risk that your preparation gets made obsolete by the very capabilities you’re preparing for.

That doesn’t mean we should ignore it. If there are things we need during an intelligence explosion that have long lead times, or bottlenecks that more capable models won’t resolve, then we should work on those now. But I’d want a fairly concrete story about why the work needs to happen in advance.

And there’s an opportunity cost. We have alignment problems we can study today, with systems we can actually run experiments on. I’m generally more excited about doing that research, learning what’s difficult, and then using increasingly capable AI systems to help us as they become available. I’m less convinced that we should put a lot of effort into designing the automation process before we know what those systems will look like.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare prosaic alignment research with capabilities research.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that AI systems would accelerate capabilities and alignment research comparably, given compute allocation.

r003.rationale: It says future models may make preparation obsolete, but does not predict that differences between alignment and capabilities research will diminish.

r004.rationale: It favors studying alignment problems with current systems and says it is less convinced by investing heavily in automation preparation before knowing what future systems will look like.
